headline: Uber lays off 10 percent of its customer service team citing AI adoption
summary: Uber's Community Operations division, its global customer support network, saw 10% of its workforce cut. The company stated the move was to "simplify operations" and "embrace AI."
details: Uber has laid off 10 percent of its global customer service team, specifically within its Community Operations division. The company cited AI adoption as a primary reason for these job cuts, aiming to simplify operations and strengthen in-person collaboration.

According to an internal memo from Uber's VP of global community operations, Megha Yethadka, the department had become "too complex and siloed." She noted that while strides have been made in using AI, an "effective organization" is needed to scale its implementation.

While Bloomberg did not specify Uber's exact generative AI applications, the article highlights recent improvements in AI agents for customer service, particularly in natural communication and understanding customer needs. Uber also reportedly mandated remote workers in the affected team to relocate to hub offices.

Uber joins a growing list of companies attributing layoffs to AI integration. Oracle cut 21,000 roles, Snap laid off 1,000 workers, and Meta reduced its workforce by 10% (8,000 jobs), subsequently moving 7,000 personnel to AI-focused organizations.

headline_marked: [[142 AI data center protests staged in 42 states]] as public opposition to buildouts increases
headline: 142 AI data center protests staged in 42 states as public opposition to buildouts increases
summary: Over 70% of Americans now oppose data centers, leading to 142 protests across 42 states. This public pushback has already delayed over $130 billion worth of projects.
details: A coordinated protest saw 142 events across 42 states, marking the first simultaneous nationwide action against data center buildouts. Organizers have branded these "unaccountable" developments as an "unacceptable infringement on our liberty."

Data centers have previously faced shortages in GPU, memory chips, and electricity infrastructure. Now, a significant challenge is the growing lack of public support, with over 70% of Americans reportedly opposing these projects.

Bipartisan political moves have led to project delays and statewide bans. More than 69 jurisdictions have imposed data center bans, including one-year moratoriums in Seattle and New York. This resistance has already delayed over $130 billion worth of data center projects by Q1 2026.

Developers have attempted to bypass opposition by choosing rural sites, securing their own power, or claiming low water usage. However, public concern persists over increased utility rates, water quality issues, and noise pollution, despite promises of jobs and tax revenue.

Future data center projects must prioritize community consent, moving beyond simple town council approvals. While the US needs data centers for the AI race, this cannot come at the expense of local quality of life. Investors must present robust plans that withstand scrutiny and account for lengthy permit processes.
